questions.question: What are the most useful functions in Go's strings package?
questions.title: Strings Package
questions.direct_answer: Contains, HasPrefix/HasSuffix, Index, Split/Join, ToUpper/ToLower, TrimSpace, Replace, Fields, Repeat, Builder. Searching, splitting, case/trim, replacing, building — the everyday text toolkit, Unicode-correct where it matters.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Strings Package beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: Contains, HasPrefix/HasSuffix, Index, Split/Join, ToUpper/ToLower, TrimSpace, Replace, Fields, Repeat, Builder.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The kit, grouped by job (all executed):

```go
// searching
strings.Contains("hello world", "wor")   // true
strings.HasPrefix("main.go", "main")   // true
strings.Index("hello", "l")             // 2 — byte offset, -1 if absent

// splitting & joining
strings.Split("a,b,c", ",")            // [a b c]
strings.Join([]string{"x","y"}, "-")    // x-y
strings.Fields("  a b  c ")             // [a b c] — any whitespace

// case & trimming
strings.ToUpper("go")                    // GO
strings.TrimSpace("  hi \n")             // hi — both ends, all whitespace

// replacing & building
strings.Replace("a-b-c", "-", "+", 2)  // a+b+c (count; -1 = all)
strings.Repeat("go", 3)                 // gogogo

var b strings.Builder
b.WriteString("hello ")
b.WriteString("world")
b.String()  // "hello world" — the loop-concat fix
```

The design notes that make this the answer rather than a list: Index returns BYTE offsets — composable with slicing (s[:idx]). Fields handles messy whitespace (the parsing case); Split is for a known delimiter. The rune-awareness: ToUpper/ToLower/Trim operate on RUNES (unicode-correct), while Index/Contains match raw byte substrings (fast, exact).

Two functions people forget and reinvent: Fields (the whitespace splitter) and Builder (the O(n) concatenator).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C[Contains Index HasPrefix - byte search]
    SP[Split Join - exact delimiter]
    FI[Fields - any whitespace run]
    TR[TrimSpace - both ends]
    BU[Builder - On building]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The function taxonomy by implementation cost: Index/Contains/HasPrefix are byte-wise substring searches (fast — the runtime uses optimized search); Split/Fields/Replace allocate (the results are new); TrimSpace/ToUpper/ToLower decode runes (Unicode-correct — the case tables come from the unicode package); Join/Repeat size their output exactly (one allocation).

The rune-vs-byte split inside one package: ToUpper/ToLower use unicode case tables — multibyte runes change correctly (é→É). Trim/TrimLeft/TrimRight accept a CUTSET (any of these runes — not a prefix!). Index/Contains match raw bytes — a pattern that happens to be invalid UTF-8 can never match inside a valid UTF-8 string (encoding boundaries align), which is why byte-search is safe for text.

The mistakes each function exists to prevent: manual whitespace loops (Fields), manual comma-joining (Join), += concatenation (Builder), manual ASCII case switching (ToUpper works on the whole range), the index-of+slicing dance for prefixes (HasPrefix reads as intent).

The missing-from-strings worth knowing: unicode/utf8 (RuneCountInString, DecodeRuneInString — the rune machinery), strings.Cut (Go 1.18 — split-once, the parsing workhorse), strings.EqualFold (case-insensitive compare), strings.Clone (the substring-anchor-breaker). Name the function for the job and the one-liner it replaced.

questions.question: What is the difference between strings.Split and strings.Fields?
questions.title: When would you use Strings Package in a real project
questions.direct_answer: Split(s, sep) — splits on an EXACT separator string (every occurrence). Fields(s) — splits on ANY whitespace (runs of spaces/tabs/newlines), ignoring leading/trailing. Split for a known delimiter; Fields for messy human text.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Split(s, sep) — splits on an EXACT separator string (every occurrence). Fields(s) — splits on ANY whitespace (runs of spaces/tabs/newlines), ignoring leading/trailing. Split for a known delimiter; Fields for messy.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The difference is the delimiter's definition:

```go
strings.Split("a,b,c", ",")        // [a b c] — exact delimiter
strings.Split(" a , b ", ",")      // [" a " " b "] — spaces PRESERVED in fields
strings.Fields("  a  b\n c ")      // [a b c] — whitespace CONSUMED
```

Executed. Split keeps whatever was between the delimiters (leading/trailing spaces stay); Fields treats any whitespace run as one boundary and drops it.

Split's edge cases that matter: splitting on an empty string yields each rune as an element (Split("abc", "") = [a b c] — the rune-split idiom); splitting a string NOT containing the delimiter yields the whole string as one element; consecutive delimiters produce EMPTY fields ("a,,b" → [a '' b]) — the CSV-vs-parsing distinction.

The choosing rule: a FORMAT you control (CSV-ish, config with a known separator) → Split, then TrimSpace the pieces if needed. HUMAN text / messy input (log parsing, splitting words) → Fields — it's Split-whitespace-runs with the trimming built in.

The third sibling: strings.SplitN(s, sep, n) bounds the count ("a,b,c,d" with n=2 → [a b,c,d]) — the 'split the first field then keep the rest' pattern for key:value parsing — and strings.Cut (Go 1.18) is the split-once primitive that returns (before, after, found).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    SP[Split on EXACT sep] --> EM[a,,b gives empty between]
    FI[Fields on whitespace RUNS] --> NM[a  b gives no empties]
    CU[Cut - split ONCE] --> BF[before, after, found]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanics of each: Split scans for the separator byte-pattern, slicing the original (the substrings SHARE the source's memory — no copies until the slice header exists), building a []string of those windows. Fields walks the bytes, finds rune-width whitespace via unicode.IsSpace, and emits the maximal non-space runs — the state machine is 'in a field / between fields,' consuming runs rather than matching single separators.

Why consecutive delimiters behave differently — the deep distinction: a delimiter is a MARKED boundary (each one creates a boundary, empty fields between adjacent ones); whitespace is a RUN (a run of any length is ONE separator). CSV's "a,,b" has a missing field (Split's empty string is the honest representation); word text's "a  b" has NO word between (Fields correctly skips). This is the split-vs-fields semantics — boundary marks vs separators — and it's why the wrong choice produces either empty strings that shouldn't exist or missing ones that should.

The Cut pattern (Go 1.18) as the primitive under the parsing world: Cut(s, sep) returns (before, after, found) — one split, no slice allocation, the natural shape for 'prefix : rest' parsing (headers, "key=value", scheme://rest). Before Cut, the idiom was Index + manual slicing with -1 checks; Cut named it. Split remains for the true-list case; Cut is for the first-separator case; Fields for the whitespace case — three delimiter semantics, three functions, and choosing by delimiter-meaning is the interview answer.

questions.question: How does strings.TrimSpace differ from strings.Trim?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Strings Package
questions.direct_answer: TrimSpace removes ALL leading/trailing whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines — Unicode-aware). Trim(s, cutset) removes leading/trailing chars that are ANY OF the cutset's runes — a set, not a substring.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: TrimSpace removes ALL leading/trailing whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines — Unicode-aware).

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Both strip from the ENDS (never the middle) — the difference is the selector:

```go
strings.TrimSpace("  \n\t hi \n ")     // "hi" — all whitespace kinds
strings.Trim("xxhiyx", "xy")           // "hi" — x's and y's from both ends
strings.Trim(".5", ".")                // "5" — decimal point stripping
```

Executed. TrimSpace has no argument — its selector is fixed (unicode.IsSpace: spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns, and the Unicode space family). Trim takes a CUTSET — a string whose RUNES are each individually removal candidates, from either end, until a non-member is hit.

The cutset misunderstanding to correct on the spot: Trim("hello", "lo") is NOT 'remove the substring lo' — it removes leading/trailing l's and o's ("he" — 'l' stripped from the end, then 'e' stops it). The cutset is a set of characters, not a pattern. For substring trimming: TrimPrefix / TrimSuffix (exact substring, once, from one side).

The family, complete: TrimSpace (whitespace), Trim (rune set), TrimPrefix/TrimSuffix (exact substring), TrimLeft/TrimRight (the one-sided variants of both). The typical input-cleaning flow: TrimSpace for user input; Trim(s, "\"'") for stripping quotes; TrimPrefix(s, "Bearer ") for auth headers.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    TS[TrimSpace - unicode whitespace]
    TR[Trim s cutset - a SET of runes]
    TP[TrimPrefix - exact substring, one side]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanics of set-based trimming: Trim decodes the cutset into a rune set (a map or filter), then scans the string's leading runes — removing each that's in the set, stopping at the first non-member — then the same from the end. It's symmetric, rune-aware (multibyte cutset members match multibyte leading runes), and allocation-returns the trimmed window (which SHARES the original's memory — the substring-anchor from the immutability topic applies to trimmed strings too).

TrimSpace's selector — unicode.IsSpace — includes the full Unicode whitespace set (the usual ASCII suspects plus non-breaking space U+00A0, ideographic space U+3000, and others) — a fact that matters when 'invisibly broken' input (a copy-pasted U+00A0 from a rich text field) fails equality checks: TrimSpace catches it, a manual trim of " \n\t" misses it. That's the Unicode-aware divide between the naive reimplementation and the stdlib.

The composable parsing idiom worth demonstrating fluency: TrimPrefix + TrimSpace + Cut chaining for real formats — TrimSpace(input) → Cut(input, ":") → Trim both parts (quotes, spaces) → parse the value. Each stage names its exact concern (outer whitespace, the structural separator, per-field cleanup), and the chain reads as the format's grammar. That composability — one job per function, ends-only, explicit selector — is the strings package's API design showing through.

questions.question: How do you replace text in a Go string — and what does the count parameter do?
questions.title: compare Strings Package with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: strings.Replace(s, old, new, n): n is how many occurrences to replace (left-to-right); -1 replaces all. For all-replacements, Go 1.12+ has ReplaceAll (same as Replace with -1).

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: strings.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Replace's signature carries the count:

```go
strings.Replace("a-b-c-d", "-", "+", 2)   // a+b+c-d — first TWO only
strings.Replace("a-b-c-d", "-", "+", -1)  // a+b+c+d — all
strings.ReplaceAll("a-b-c-d", "-", "+")    // a+b+c+d — the -1 named
```

Executed. The count is left-to-right — the 'first N' occurrences. -1 is the all-sentinel. ReplaceAll (Go 1.12) is Replace(s, o, n, -1) with a name — use it for the common case; keep Replace for partial replacement (the first occurrence only: n=1).

The return, always: a NEW string (immutable — of course). If old doesn't appear, the ORIGINAL string is returned — a free no-op, no allocation (the runtime checks before building).

The regex boundary: Replace handles LITERAL substrings. When the 'what to replace' is a pattern (all digits, word boundaries, case-insensitive) — that's regexp.ReplaceAllString, the heavier tool (compile once, reuse; ~10-50x slower than strings.Replace, per docs' own guidance).

The multibyte honesty: old and new are substrings matched in bytes — replacement of multibyte runes works exactly (the whole rune's bytes match), and the count counts OCCURRENCES of the whole old string, never partial byte overlaps.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R[Replace s old new n] --> |n=2| P[first 2 only]
    R --> |-1| A[all]
    RA[ReplaceAll] --> A
    NO[no match] --> OR[returns ORIGINAL - zero alloc]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The implementation tiers behind Replace: for the no-match case, the original pointer returns (zero cost). For small counts, the scan-replace builds incrementally. The workhorse underneath is strings.genReplace — a single generalized implementation serving Replace, ReplaceAll, and (via a different entry) the Title/Builder paths — with the count threading through as the loop bound.

Why the count exists at all (API archaeology): pre-strings-function libraries (C's strncpy world, sed's g flag) made 'replace first N' a real operation — Go kept the explicit n because partial replacement is genuinely common: 'replace the first occurrence of the placeholder', 'escape the first quote.' The -1-all sentinel plus the later ReplaceAll naming is the API evolving toward the common case without breaking the general one — the same pattern as fmt's %v and %-specific verbs.

The regexp crossover deserves the numbers interviewers respect: strings.Replace is a substring search (Boyer-Moore-ish) with a straight build; regexp compiles the pattern (compile ONCE, outside the loop — the classic mistake is compiling per call), backtracks or automata-matches, and allocates captures. The docs' own performance note: for literal replacements, strings.Replace; for patterns, regexp — and 'literal' includes FIXED separators in untrusted input (a delimiter in a config format is literal even though the input varies). The wrong-tool bugs: regexp for literal work (10-50x slow, allocation-heavy) and Replace for pattern work (can't express 'all digits' at all).

questions.question: How do you efficiently build a string from many pieces in Go?
questions.title: debug a problem involving Strings Package
questions.direct_answer: strings.Builder — WriteString per piece, String() once at the end. O(n) total. The anti-pattern is += in a loop: O(n²). For separators between pieces: strings.Join (sizes the result exactly, one allocation).

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: strings.Builder — WriteString per piece, String() once at the end. O(n) total. The anti-pattern is += in a loop: O(n²). For separators between pieces: strings.Join (sizes the result exactly, one.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The Builder pattern (executed):

```go
var b strings.Builder
for _, piece := range pieces {
    b.WriteString(piece)
}
s := b.String()   // one final copy
```

Builder is a []byte internally with append's amortized growth — WriteString is O(1) amortized; String() copies ONCE at the end. Total: O(n) with ~2n bytes touched.

The separator case has a specialist: strings.Join(pieces, ",") — it PRE-COMPUTES the exact final length (sum + separators) and allocates once, then copies. Zero re-allocation, zero over-allocation. When the output is joined-with-sep, Join beats the Builder loop.

The format case: fmt.Sprintf composes text+values — but 3-5x the cost (runtime format parsing). The hybrid for readable + fast: build static parts with Builder, insert values with strconv (Itoa, FormatFloat) — the pattern every fast logger uses.

The hierarchy, by job: Join (separator-delimited list — exact-size, one alloc) → Builder (arbitrary accumulation — amortized, one final copy) → Sprintf (formatted composition — readable, slowest) → += (NEVER in a loop — O(n²), the canonical Go perf bug).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    PLUS[+= in loop] --> O2[On2]
    B[Builder] --> G[grow buffer + one final copy] --> O1[On]
    J[Join] --> EX[pre-computes exact size - one alloc]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The allocation math each tool chooses: += copies the accumulated prefix on EVERY iteration (k pieces → k(k-1)/2 bytes — quadratic). Builder grows a buffer (amortized doubling — total copies ≈ 2n, linear) and pays one final string conversion. Join does arithmetic (sum of lengths + sep count), allocates EXACTLY, and writes each piece — no growth, no final re-copy (Join builds... actually it builds the byte result then converts — one alloc, one write pass). The three strategies — quadratic, amortized-linear, exact-linear — are the same trade array-growth vs pre-sizing vs naive-append makes, resurfacing in string space.

Builder's zero-copy Read/Write integration: Builder implements io.Writer — fmt.Fprintf(&b, ...) writes formatted output INTO the builder (the Sprintf cost without the intermediate string). That composes the format engine with the efficient buffer — the 'readable and fast' middle tier. And Builder.String() returns the accumulated string WITHOUT copying... no — it copies into a new string (the internal bytes stay for further writes). The Copy checks: strings.Builder panics on Write after String (the copy-out contract) — the API makes the one-conversion discipline structural.

The bytes.Buffer sibling and the choosing rule: Buffer when the data is/should-be bytes (it converts to []byte for free at .Bytes() — no string conversion at all if bytes were the goal); Builder when a STRING is the final product (the compiler knows Builder is string-bound and can skip UTF-8 validation paths Buffer pays). Both are the growth strategy; the destination type is the choice — and that boundary (string vs bytes) is the same one the immutability topic drew.
